- **Last Friday I had the pleasure of attending the Communiqué Awards ceremony, having spent the previous weeks on the judging panel. - **We talk a lot in medical affairs about clinical evidence. But increasingly, I think we also need to talk about what happens when strong evidence alone isn’t enough. Over the last six months, I’ve been working across a pipeline of vaccine assets, and one thing has become very clear to me: Many office-based medical affairs professionals are highly trained in science, but far fewer are trained to think about cost-effectiveness and healthcare system value. In markets like the UK, that matters enormously. Market access considerations aren’t just something to address at the end of development. They shape the questions that need to be asked from the very beginning: – Which outcomes are truly meaningful? – What comparators will matter? – What evidence gaps could later affect adoption, reimbursement or implementation? I’m not talking about MSLs here. I’m talking about medical strategy. The people shaping evidence generation plans, trial endpoints, and clinical narratives at pipeline stage. This doesn’t mean medical affairs and HEOR should become the same function. But I do think the future of medical affairs will require greater fluency in how clinical value translates into system value. Because we’ve all seen assets with genuinely strong efficacy data struggle at the point of access - not because the science wasn’t compelling, but because the value story wasn’t built alongside it. Medical affairs sits in a uniquely powerful position between science, clinicians, and the healthcare system itself. The opportunity now is to strengthen that position even further by developing broader understanding of access, health economics and system priorities earlier in the process. To me, that feels less like scope creep and more like the natural evolution of modern medical affairs. Your thoughts are welcome! PS happy bank holiday weekend🌷 ...more**

- **A couple of weeks ago, an elderly neighbour fell outside my house. After assessing her injuries and realising the ambulance wait would be long, I drove her to A&E myself. There’s something about NHS hospitals that never really leaves you - the look of the corridors, the sounds, the (sometimes questionable) smells. It immediately brought back memories of the people I worked with, the camaraderie, the sheer volume of knowledge you absorb so quickly in those environments. Healthcare can be stressful, overwhelming and emotionally heavy. But the feeling you get when you genuinely help someone at a vulnerable moment in their life is unmatched. My neighbour is absolutely fine now and we’ve actually become friends - we text most days and she’s invited me over for dinner. Moments like that remind me that even though I no longer work on the frontline, the patient-centred part of me never disappeared. And honestly, moving into pharma didn’t diminish that. If anything, it expanded it. Because despite what people sometimes assume, there are incredibly talented, hardworking people across this industry dedicating their careers to bringing innovation into healthcare systems and improving patient outcomes at scale. - **Hot take incoming. About psychometric tests. Colour Insights is brilliant for understanding how you show up in a room and how to adapt to the people around you. It helps you to understand why working with some people feels more natural than with others, and how to adjust your communication style to foster a better team dynamic. However I think the most underrated one is Clifton Strengths. Most feedback culture focuses on the gaps. What are your blind spots? Where do you need to improve? That is certainly important, and I’m not dismissing it, but Clifton Strengths flips the question entirely. It asks what are you actually great at and encourages you to think about if, and how, you’re working with them. There’s evidence in psychology that when children are told they’re intelligent, they perform better. I think the same thing happens here. Name your strengths and you start to own them differently. My top three: Futuristic, Strategic, Connectedness. Since having accurate words to use to describe my strengths, I’ve been more intentional about leaning in. Turns out being a Medical Lead for a multi-asset vaccine pipeline makes a lot of sense for someone who thinks in futures, finds paths through complexity and sees how everything connects. Who knew! Keen to hear what others think about the best and most useful psychometric tests, and what your strengths are. If you’re feeling a little lost or not enjoying your current role - think about whether you’re work is aligned to your strengths. If not, how can you dial them up?💡 ...more**

- **I did everything right - and my student loan balance has barely moved. I was the first person in my family to go to university. I couldn’t have gone without a student loan - it wasn’t a choice between options. It was the only option. Before I’d even started, the system wasn’t fair. I was denied a maintenance bursary because my mother had recently moved in with my stepfather, and his salary pushed the household income above the threshold. He was not my parent. He had, rightfully so, never contributed to my education or my living costs. The system treated his income as a proxy for my support regardless. That’s not an edge case. That’s a design flaw. I studied pharmacy - a four-year Masters degree, not by choice but by professional requirement, at £9,000 a year. I worked throughout my entire degree at Boots Pharmacy to supplement my maintenance loan. I graduated with a first-class honours. I went straight into the NHS, where I stayed for four years. I’ve spent the last several years in the pharmaceutical industry. I’ve worked exceptionally hard for every step of this career - because I knew there was no safety net if I didn’t. And since I started my career as a pharmacist I’ve been watching a number that barely moves. I left university with approximately £65,000 in student loan debt. Nearly a decade later, my balance is £56,000. Every month I repay about £400 after tax and national insurance. Less than £50 of that reduces my actual debt. Over the last few years my interest rate has sat at almost 8% (RPI plus 3%). I’ve repaid less than £9,000 in capital through nearly ten years of hard work and regular monthly repayments. My concern isn’t just the repayment threshold - though freezing it while inflation rises is a form of double standard that shouldn’t go unexamined. My concern is the interest rate itself. RPI has been formally discontinued by the ONS as a measure of general inflation because of its known flaws. It is still used to calculate student loan interest - and then a further 3% is added on top. These are not commercial loans taken out voluntarily in a competitive market. They are the only mechanism available to people who want to access higher education. Especially people from working class backgrounds. So I’ll ask the question plainly: who profits from this and what public interest does that serve? If this is what the system looks like for people who do everything right - what message does that send to the next generation about whether university, and the debt that comes with it, is worth it? And how is this system encouraging social mobility? The parliamentary inquiry is open for evidence submissions until 14 April 2025. If this resonates with your experience, I’d encourage you to submit: https://lnkd.in/e8X7AS6p If you’ve already submitted or have a view on this and want to discuss, my inbox is open #plan2studentloan ...more**

- **Happy Wednesday to my wonderful LinkedIn network 👋🏼 I wanted to share a few reflections now that I’m almost two months into my new role (how are we nearly in March already?!). Firstly - how you approach your first 90 days really does shape your longer-term success. Before I started, Shelley Watcham recommended reading The First 90 Days by Michael Watkins - and it was great advice. - **𝗪𝗵𝗲𝗻 𝗧𝘄𝗼 𝗞𝗢𝗟𝘀 𝗗𝗶𝘀𝗮𝗴𝗿𝗲𝗲, 𝗠𝗼𝘀𝘁 𝗠𝗦𝗟𝘀 𝗗𝗼 𝗘𝘅𝗮𝗰𝘁𝗹𝘆 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝗪𝗿𝗼𝗻𝗴 𝗧𝗵𝗶𝗻𝗴 I've watched this exact scenario play out more times than I can count. An MSL meets with Dr. Chen on Monday. She's convinced Biomarker X will change clinical practice. She has retrospective data. She's confident. She's credible. On Wednesday, the same MSL meets Prof. Miller. He calls Biomarker X "noise." He has mechanistic arguments. He's equally confident. Equally credible. Now what? The easy move is to pick a winner. The routine move is to record both opinions as "insights" and move on. The Medical Affairs move is different. Recognize that the disagreement itself may be the insight. Conflicting KOL opinions are not necessarily a problem to resolve. They can be a signal that you've reached the edge of current evidence. And that's exactly where Medical Affairs creates disproportionate value. When I think about this situation, I come back to two questions: What would need to be true for Dr. Chen to change her mind? And: What would need to be true for Prof. Miller to change his? The answers can reveal something much more valuable than simply knowing who supports Biomarker X and who doesn't. They can help map the evidence gap: • What data are missing? • What questions should be explored in future studies or advisory boards? • Where is the uncertainty greatest? • What does the clinical community actually need to know? The goal isn't to make everyone agree. The goal is to understand why reasonable experts disagree. Because that disagreement may tell us where science needs to go next. KOL disagreements are not noise. They're coordinates. Most MSLs collect opinions. The best ones map uncertainty. When was the last time you mapped uncertainty instead of simply documenting disagreement? #MedicalAffairs #MSL #FieldMedical #KOL #Pharma**

- **Medical Affairs leadership just got harder to hire for. Here’s why that’s the wrong problem to solve. The old model rewarded depth. A strong scientific mind. Deep therapeutic expertise. Someone who could hold their own with a KOL. That’s now the entry fee, not the differentiator. Today’s Medical Affairs leaders are expected to carry scientific credibility, strategic influence and commercial awareness at the same time, while staying firmly inside the compliance line. That combination is rare. So searches drag, shortlists thin, and everyone blames a talent shortage. It isn’t a talent shortage. It’s a development gap. Four capabilities are separating the Medical Affairs leaders who thrive from the ones who plateau: - Integrative judgement. Weighing the science, the strategy and the compliance boundary in a single decision, not passing each to a different function. - AI discernment. Knowing when to trust what a model produces and when not to, and leading MSL teams through that shift without hype or fear. The scientific rigor that defines Medical Affairs is exactly what makes this judgement possible. - Change resilience. Guiding field teams through constant reinvention while protecting them from the burnout that comes with it. - Scientific storytelling. Turning complex evidence into a clear insight that shapes cross-functional strategy, and lands with a leadership team that isn’t in the data every day. None of these appear on a CV. They’re built, deliberately, inside the function, over time and they’re built through re-emagining what to look for in the hiring process That’s the uncomfortable truth for Medical Affairs. You can’t recruit your way out of a capability gap. You develop your way through it. Frameworks don’t build capability. People do. #Qinexa**

- **August 8th is International Cat Day! 🐈‍⬛🩷 This day is about celebrating our cats and encouraging adoption as they deserve just as much love as we give our dogs. Looking back, here's what we noticed in Henry before his diagnosis: • Matted fur • Increased hunger • Weight loss • Increased thirst We did everything we could - weekly vet visits, careful diet management, and gradually adjusted insulin over several months - but by the time we caught it, it had already progressed too far. - **"Do you think AI will replace your job as an MSL?" That question came from a Year 12 student at Harris Lowe Academy Willesden, where I spent a morning talking to students about life after sixth form and careers in both pharmacy and life sciences. I said yes to this one instantly, because when I was in sixth form, I had no idea the life sciences sector existed, let alone Medical Affairs. So I told them my story honestly, from feeling lost during sixth form, to university, to the three career moves I've made since. If you've heard me speak before, you'll know I skipped the polished, didactic stuff. Instead, we spent time talking about the twists, wrong turns and lessons that don't usually make it onto a CV. It was heartwarming to see so many students excited about healthcare and life sciences. But my favourite moments were with the ones interested in business and economics, showing them there's a place for them here too. They're growing up with pressures a lot of us never faced: 🤖 Thinking about how AI will shape their future careers long before they've even started them 📈 A brutally competitive graduate job market 📱 Constant comparison through social media and the pressure to have it all figured out Back to that AI question. My answer: AI will change how we work, in many ways it already has, but the human side of Medical Affairs, trust, nuance, real relationships, will always matter. The skill is learning to work alongside it, not compete with it. Moments like this remind me why it matters to show young people careers they might never stumble across on their own. Sometimes all it takes is hearing that a job exists. Thank you to the Harris Futures , Ingrid Leake and Ramanpreet Bains for the invite and the warm welcome. If you're a school, university, or organisation looking for someone to speak about careers in life sciences or navigating an unconventional career journey, I'd love to hear from you. Feel free to drop me a message. #LifeSciences #STEMCareers #CareerDevelopment #FutureTalent #PublicSpeaking**
